pattern.none: no regular measure: أَوَّل declines like an elative أَفْعَل (diptote, feminine أُولَى), but its root is disputed (و أ ل or أ و ل)

derivedFrom.none: suppletive: “first” is not made from وَاحِد “one”

plurals.note: the first ones; the top ones (الْأَوَائِلُ “the best students”)

profile.feeling: The first day of school, the first step.

senses.def: first (before a noun in a construct: أَوَّلُ يَوْمٍ; after it like an adjective: الْيَوْمُ الْأَوَّلُ)

examples.text: هٰذَا أَوَّلُ يَوْمٍ لِي فِي الْعَمَلِ.
examples.tr: This is my first day at work.
The first lesson is easy.
This is my first visit to Cairo.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: first; also the noun “first part, beginning”. It is not formed from وَاحِد “one”: the ordinal of one is a word of its own. It declines like the elatives (أَفْعَل): a diptote, with the feminine أُولَى.

pitfalls: “First” does not come from وَاحِد: it is أَوَّل (m.) / أُولَى (f.) — but one o’clock is السَّاعَةُ الْوَاحِدَةُ.
A diptote: without the article and outside a construct it takes no tanwīn (أَوَّلُ, accusative and genitive أَوَّلَ); in a construct it declines normally: فِي أَوَّلِ يَوْمٍ “on the first day”.
subtleties: Two positions: before the noun in a construct (أَوَّلُ مَرَّةٍ, أَوَّلُ يَوْمٍ) or after it as an adjective (الْمَرَّةُ الْأُولَى, الْيَوْمُ الْأَوَّلُ) — both mean “the first time / day”.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: أَوَّل is the only word for “first”; بِدَايَة is “beginning” (a noun) and أَوَّلِيّ “initial, primary”.
funFacts: أَوَّلًا “firstly” and الْأَوَائِل “the top students” are built on the same word.

plurals.note: rare: ordinals are seldom used in the plural

examples.tr: I live on the second floor.
Take the second street on the right.
It is two o’clock now.

etymology.text: From the root ث ن ي of اِثْنَان “two”, pattern فَاعِل (Wiktionary: second). A defective adjective: ثَانٍ, ثَانِيًا, الثَّانِي.

pitfalls: A defective adjective: indefinite ثَانٍ (nominative and genitive), ثَانِيًا (accusative); definite الثَّانِي, accusative الثَّانِيَ.
The feminine ثَانِيَة is also a noun: “a second” (of time).
subtleties: The second is the one ordinal with a weak last root letter: its masculine looks different (ثَانٍ, الثَّانِي) while the feminine is regular (ثَانِيَة).
profile.synonymsNone: An ordinal has no synonym: it is the only word for its place in a row. Related words are the fraction of the same root and the adverb in -an (“firstly, secondly …”).
funFacts: ثَانِيَة “a second” of time is “the second (division)” of the minute, as دَقِيقَة “minute” is “the fine (division)” of the hour.

profile.feeling: Bronze; the third in a row.

examples.tr: My son is in the third year (of school).
It is three o’clock now.
He came third (lit. in the third place).

etymology.text: From the root ث ل ث of ثَلَاثَة “three”, on the pattern فَاعِل (Wiktionary: third). The fraction ثُلُث “a third” shares the root.

pitfalls: ثَالِث has a long ā after the first letter (ṯāliṯ); the fraction is ثُلُث “a third”.
No gender polarity: the ordinal agrees like any adjective — الْيَوْمُ الثَّالِثُ, السَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ (but three days = ثَلَاثَةُ أَيَّامٍ).
subtleties: The third of the month is الثَّالِثُ مِنَ الشَّهْرِ: the day (الْيَوْم) is masculine, so the ordinal is too.
profile.synonymsNone: An ordinal has no synonym: it is the only word for its place in a row. Related words are the fraction of the same root and the adverb in -an (“firstly, secondly …”).
funFacts: The proverb الثَّالِثَةُ ثَابِتَةٌ “the third (time) holds” is said before a third try.

examples.tr: My room is on the fourth floor.

examples.text: كَانَ الْيَوْمُ الرَّابِعُ أَجْمَلَ يَوْمٍ فِي الرِّحْلَةِ.
examples.tr: The fourth day was the best day of the trip.
We meet at four o’clock.

etymology.text: From the root ر ب ع of أَرْبَعَة “four”, pattern فَاعِل (Wiktionary: fourth). رُبْع “a quarter” and الْأَرْبِعَاء “Wednesday” share the root.

pitfalls: The ordinal has no أ: أَرْبَعَة “four” but رَابِع “fourth”.
رَابِع (fourth) and رُبْع (a quarter) share the root but are different words.
subtleties: Wednesday, الْأَرْبِعَاء, is “the fourth (day)” of the week that starts on Sunday.
profile.synonymsNone: An ordinal has no synonym: it is the only word for its place in a row. Related words are the fraction of the same root and the adverb in -an (“firstly, secondly …”).

examples.tr: The lecture starts at five o’clock.
This is his fifth birthday.
Today is the fifth of May.

etymology.text: From the root خ م س of خَمْسَة “five”, pattern فَاعِل (Wiktionary: fifth). The fraction خُمُس “a fifth” shares the root.

pitfalls: خ is a moon letter: الْخَامِسُ is al-ḫāmisu (the l is heard).
No polarity: الْيَوْمُ الْخَامِسُ, السَّاعَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ.
subtleties: Thursday, الْخَمِيس, is “the fifth (day)” — the same root.

plurals.note: rare: ordinals are seldom used in the plural

examples.tr: I wake up at six o’clock.
My father works on the sixth floor.
She is in the sixth year (of school).

etymology.text: From the root س د س (Wiktionary: sixth); the cardinal سِتَّة belongs to the same root, with the د assimilated to the following consonant (sitt-). The fraction سُدُس “a sixth” keeps the د.

pitfalls: The ordinal has a د that the cardinal does not show: سِتَّة “six” but سَادِس “sixth”, سُدُس “a sixth”.
subtleties: الْحَاسَّةُ السَّادِسَةُ is “the sixth sense”, as in many languages.

profile.feeling: The last day of the week — and seventh heaven.

examples.text: السَّبْتُ هُوَ الْيَوْمُ السَّابِعُ مِنَ الْأُسْبُوعِ.
examples.tr: Saturday is the seventh day of the week.
We have dinner at seven o’clock.
I’m in seventh heaven!

etymology.text: From the root س ب ع of سَبْعَة “seven”, pattern فَاعِل (Wiktionary: seventh). أُسْبُوع “week” and سُبُع “a seventh” share the root.

pitfalls: سَابِع (sābiʿ, seventh) and سَبْع (sabʿ, seven — feminine counting form) look alike: the long ā marks the ordinal.
subtleties: In the Arab week (from Sunday, الْأَحَد “the first”) Saturday is the seventh day.
profile.synonymsNone: An ordinal has no synonym: it is the only word for its place in a row. Related words are the fraction of the same root and the adverb in -an (“firstly, secondly …”).

profile.feeling: The start of the working day.

examples.tr: Work hours start at eight o’clock.
My daughter is in the eighth year (of school).
August is the eighth month.

etymology.text: From the root ث م ن of ثَمَانِيَة “eight”, pattern فَاعِل (Wiktionary: eighth). The fraction ثُمُن “an eighth” shares the root.

pitfalls: The ordinal has no ي: ثَمَانِيَة “eight” but ثَامِن “eighth”.
subtleties: ثَمَن “price” is written with the same three letters but is a different word: ثَمَنٌ / ثَامِنٌ.
profile.synonymsNone: An ordinal has no synonym: it is the only word for its place in a row. Related words are the fraction of the same root and the adverb in -an (“firstly, secondly …”).

examples.tr: The train arrived at nine o’clock.
September is the ninth month.
He lived in the ninth century.

etymology.text: From the root ت س ع of تِسْعَة “nine”, pattern فَاعِل (Wiktionary: ninth). The fraction تُسُع “a ninth” shares the root.

pitfalls: تَاسِع (tāsiʿ, ninth) and تِسْع (tisʿ, nine — feminine counting form): the long ā marks the ordinal.
subtleties: The ninth month of the Islamic calendar is Ramadan: الشَّهْرُ التَّاسِعُ in the Hijri year.

profile.feeling: Bedtime — and the tenth time of saying it.

examples.tr: This is the tenth time!
I live on the tenth floor.
We go to bed at ten o’clock.

etymology.text: From the root ع ش ر of عَشَرَة “ten”, pattern فَاعِل (Wiktionary: tenth). عُشْر “a tenth” and عِشْرُونَ “twenty” share the root.

pitfalls: ع is a moon letter: الْعَاشِرُ is al-ʿāširu.
The same letters spell the form III verb عَاشَرَ “to keep company with” (Wiktionary) — the vowels tell them apart.
subtleties: Above ten the ordinals are compounds: الْحَادِيَ عَشَرَ “the eleventh”, الثَّانِيَ عَشَرَ “the twelfth”; from twenty on they look like the cardinal with the article: الْعِشْرُونَ “the twentieth”.
profile.synonymsNone: An ordinal has no synonym: it is the only word for its place in a row. Related words are the fraction of the same root and the adverb in -an (“firstly, secondly …”).

derivedFrom.none: a basic adjective of the root أ خ ر (behind, after)

plurals.note: the last ones; in news style “the latter”

profile.feeling: The last page, the last train home.

senses.def: latest, most recent (الْأَيَّامُ الْأَخِيرَةُ “the last few days”)

examples.tr: This is the last lesson.
We got off at the last station.

examples.text: فِي الْأَيَّامِ الْأَخِيرَةِ كَانَ الْجَوُّ حَارًّا.
examples.tr: In the last few days the weather was hot.

synonyms.nuance: last — before the noun, in a construct: آخِرُ يَوْمٍ, آخِرُ مَرَّةٍ

etymology.text: Root أ خ ر “to be behind, to come after”; Wiktionary: last, final; last, latest, most recent. آخِر “last”, آخَر “other” and تَأَخَّرَ “to be late” share the root.

pitfalls: آخِر (ʾāḫir, “last”) and آخَر (ʾāḫar, “other”) differ in one vowel: آخِرُ يَوْمٍ “the last day” / يَوْمٌ آخَرُ “another day”.
أَخِير follows its noun like any adjective: الدَّرْسُ الْأَخِيرُ “the last lesson”.
subtleties: Two ways to say “the last day”: الْيَوْمُ الْأَخِيرُ (adjective after the noun) or آخِرُ يَوْمٍ (آخِر before the noun, in a construct).
funFacts: مُتَأَخِّرًا “late” and الْآخِرَة “the hereafter, the last abode” come from the same root.

profile.feeling: An apple cut in two; half an hour of waiting.

examples.tr: It is half past three.
I ate half the apple.
Half of the students are from Egypt.

synonyms.nuance: half, part — one half of a line of verse is a شَطْر

etymology.text: Root ن ص ف; Wiktionary: half, a half, semi-, hemi-; middle; also written نُصْف. إِنْصَاف “fairness” belongs to the same root.

funFacts: إِنْصَاف “fairness, justice” is from the same root: being fair is giving each one his half.
pitfalls: نِصْف is a noun: it stands before what it halves, in a construct: نِصْفُ سَاعَةٍ “half an hour” (not *سَاعَةٌ نِصْفٌ).
Wiktionary also gives نُصْف (with u); the usual form is نِصْف.
subtleties: In clock times it takes the article: الثَّالِثَةُ وَالنِّصْفُ “half past three”; with amounts “and a half” is وَنِصْفٌ: سَاعَةٌ وَنِصْفٌ “an hour and a half”.

profile.feeling: A quarter of an hour — enough for a coffee.

senses.def: a quarter, a fourth (in clock times: وَالرُّبْعُ “a quarter past”, إِلَّا رُبْعًا “a quarter to”)

examples.tr: It is a quarter past five.
I waited a quarter of an hour for you!
We only ate a quarter of the cake.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: رُبْع is the only word for a fourth part, as ثُلُث is for a third and خُمُس for a fifth.

etymology.text: Root ر ب ع of أَرْبَعَة “four”; Wiktionary: one fourth, one quarter; quarter (area, region); written رُبُع or رُبْع; cognate with Hebrew רֹבַע (rova, “quarter”).

funFacts: The great sand desert of the Arabian Peninsula is الرُّبْعُ الْخَالِي, “the Empty Quarter”.
pitfalls: “A quarter to” is إِلَّا رُبْعًا (lit. “less a quarter”, accusative): الرَّابِعَةُ إِلَّا رُبْعًا “a quarter to four”.
subtleties: Two vowellings: رُبْع (rubʿ, the usual one) and رُبُع (rubuʿ, classical); both are correct.

profile.feeling: Old stones, history books, a hundred years.

examples.tr: We live in the twenty-first century.
This palace was built two centuries ago.
He lived in the nineteenth century.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ḳarn- “horn” (Wiktionary: horn; century). The meaning “century” may come from “people of the same age”; Wiktionary also mentions a possible loan from Greek χρόνος (“time”).

funFacts: ذُو الْقَرْنَيْنِ, “the one with the two horns”, is a king in the Qurʾān, often identified with Alexander the Great.
pitfalls: قَرْن is also “horn” (of an animal); the plural قُرُون serves both.
subtleties: Centuries take the ordinal: الْقَرْنُ الْعَاشِرُ “the tenth century”; from twenty on the ordinal is the cardinal with the article: الْقَرْنُ الْعِشْرُونَ.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: Ten years in one word; a signature at the bottom of a page.

examples.tr: I lived in Cairo for a whole decade.

examples.text: تَغَيَّرَتِ الْمَدِينَةُ كَثِيرًا فِي الْعَقْدِ الْأَخِيرِ.
examples.tr: The city changed a lot in the last decade.
I signed the work contract yesterday.

synonyms.nuance: ten years — said out, the everyday way

etymology.text: The verbal noun of عَقَدَ “to tie, to knot”; Wiktionary: tying, binding; tie, bond; contract, covenant; decade; denary number. A decade is a “knot” of ten.

funFacts: عِقْد (ʿiqd, with i) is a necklace — beads tied on a string; عُقْدَة (ʿuqda) is a knot or a complex.
pitfalls: عَقْد (ʿaqd: decade, contract) is not عِقْد (ʿiqd: necklace); the plural عُقُود serves all of them.
subtleties: In everyday speech a decade is mostly عَشْرُ سَنَوَاتٍ; عَقْد is the written word.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses ذِكْرَى only as “remembrance, recollection, memory”; as “anniversary” it is the usual word (الذِّكْرَى السَّنَوِيَّة, ذِكْرَى الزَّوَاج), the day of remembrance of an event.

profile.feeling: Candles, old photos, a date in the calendar.

senses.def: anniversary — the day that recalls an event (الذِّكْرَى السَّنَوِيَّةُ)

examples.tr: Today is my parents’ wedding anniversary.
The school celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of its founding.
Tomorrow we celebrate the company’s tenth anniversary.

synonyms.nuance: feast, festive day — عِيدُ الزَّوَاجِ is also “wedding anniversary”

etymology.text: Root ذ ك ر “to remember, to mention”; Wiktionary: remembrance, recollection, memory; plural ذِكْرَيَات “reminiscences, memoirs”. An anniversary is a day of remembrance.

funFacts: The plural ذِكْرَيَات “memories” is a favourite word of Arabic songs.
pitfalls: ذِكْرَى ends in alif maqṣūra: it never shows the case (ذِكْرَى in all three cases) and takes no tanwīn.
subtleties: The first meaning of ذِكْرَى is “memory, remembrance” (ذِكْرَى جَمِيلَةٌ “a beautiful memory”); the anniversary is the day that brings the memory back.
